title: Fluorescence Biomembrane Force Probe: Concurrent Quantitation of Receptor-ligand Kinetics and Binding-induced Intracellular Signaling on a Single Cell
protocol: Obtain 8-10 μl of blood from finger prick.
Add to 1 ml of carbonate/bicarbonate buffer.
Gently vortex or pipette the mixture.
Centrifuge for 1 min at 900 x g.
Discard supernatant and wash once more.
Weigh 3.5-4 mg of Biotin-PEG3500-NHS linker.
Dissolve it in carbonate/bicarbonate buffer to make a final concentration of 3 mg/ml.
Mix 171 μl of carbonate/bicarbonate buffer, 10 μl of RBC pack, and 1049 μl of Biotin-PEG3500-NHS linker solution.
Incubate at room temperature for 30 min.
Wash the RBC once with carbonate/bicarbonate buffer.
Wash the RBC twice with N2-5% buffer.
Place the linker bottle with loosened cap in a glass vacuum desiccator filled with desiccants.
Vacuum for 5 min.
Fill the desiccator with argon.
Tighten the cap and take the bottle out.
Seal the bottle with plastic paraffin film.
Store in -20 °C.
Dilute nystatin into N2-5% buffer to make a final concentration of 40 µg/ml.
Mix 5 µl of biotinylated RBC with 71.4 µl of nystatin solution and incubate for 1 hr at 0 °C.
Wash twice with N2-5% buffer.
Store the mixture with N2-5% buffer + 0.5% BSA in the refrigerator (4 °C).
Weigh 50 mg of glass beads powder and re-suspend them in 500 µl of DI water.
Mix 0.5 ml of 30% H2O2 with 9.5 ml of DI water in a 50 ml beaker, then add 2 ml of concentrated NH4OH.
Bring this solution to a boil on a hot plate and add the glass beads.
Continue to boil for another 5 min, gently swirling every minute.
Transfer ~5 ml of this hot bead suspension into a 15 ml micro-centrifuge tube and top up with RT DI water.
Centrifuge at 3,500 x g for 5 min, remove and discard the supernatant.
Transfer another 5 ml of hot bead suspension to washed beads, top up with more DI water, mix well, and centrifuge again.
Repeat washing procedure until about 50 ml of DI water is used, which will be a total of 4 to 5 times.
Transfer the bead suspension into a 1 ml vial.
Wash the beads three times with methanol by centrifugation at 17,000 x g for 5 minutes each time.
Re-suspend the beads in 1 ml of 100% methanol.
Add 45.6 ml of methanol to a 50 ml centrifuge tube.
Add 0.4 ml of acetic acid to the tube.
Add 1.85 ml of DI water to the tube.
Add 1.15 ml of 3-Mercaptopropyltrimethoxysilane (MPTMS) to the tube.
Add 1 ml of bead suspension prepared in step 2.1 to the tube.
Incubate the mixture at room temperature for 3 hours.
Wash the beads once with fresh methanol after incubation.
Re-suspend the beads into 500 μl of methanol.
Evenly divide the concentrated glass bead suspension among a set of 20 dry and clean glass vials.
Evaporate off the methanol using a jet of dry argon while rotating the vials.
Place the vials in a pre-heated drying oven at 120 °C for 5 minutes.
Loosely place caps on the vials after taking them out of the oven.
Vacuum the desiccator with a vacuum pump until cooled, then purge it with dry argon to normal atmospheric pressure.
Quickly re-tighten the cap(s) on the vial after removing the lid from the desiccator.
Seal the vials with plastic paraffin film.
Store the sealed vials at room temperature in a dry dark storage box.
Wash one vial of dry beads once with phosphate buffer.
Resuspend the washed beads into 50 µl of phosphate buffer and store at 4°C.
Weigh 2-3 mg of MAL-PEG3500-NHS linker and dissolve it in carbonate/bicarbonate buffer to reach a final concentration of 0.231 mg/ml.
Mix an equal volume of protein stock with carbonate/bicarbonate buffer to make Solution 1.
Incubate the mixture of Solution 1 and an equal volume of MAL-PEG3500-NHS linker solution at room temperature for 30 min.
Vacuum dry the MAL-PEG3500-NHS linker bottle in a glass vacuum desiccator filled with desiccants for 5 minutes.
Fill the desiccator with argon, tighten the cap of the linker bottle, and seal it with plastic paraffin film.
Store the sealed linker bottle in a container with desiccants at -20°C.
Mix 5 µl of MPTMS beads with Solution 2.
Add phosphate buffer to make a final volume of 250 μl.
Incubate the beads overnight at room temperature.
Wash the beads three times with phosphate buffer.
Re-suspend into 100 μl of phosphate buffer and store at 4 °C.
Mix 5 µl of MPTMS beads with Solution 2.
Add 5 µl of 4 mg/ml Streptavidin−Maleimide (SA-MAL) solution.
Add phosphate buffer to make a final volume of 250 μl.
Incubate the beads overnight at room temperature.
Wash the beads three times with phosphate buffer.
Re-suspend into 100 µl of phosphate buffer and store at 4 °C.
Mix 5 µl of MPTMS beads with 5 µl of 4 mg/ml Streptavidin solution.
Add 140 µl of phosphate buffer.
Incubate the beads overnight at room temperature.
Wash the beads three times with phosphate buffer.
Re-suspend into 50 µl of phosphate buffer and store at 4 °C.
Mix 5 µl of SA coated beads with a biotinylated protein (volume depending on desired coating density).
Add phosphate buffer to make a final volume of 100 μl.
Incubate the mixture overnight at 4 °C or for 3 hours at room temperature.
Wash the beads three times with phosphate buffer.
Re-suspend into 50 µl of phosphate buffer and store at 4 °C.
Cut long capillary glass tubes into short pieces of around 3 inches in length.
Mount one piece onto the micropipette puller and click the “Pull” button to heat the middle of the capillary, pulling it on both ends to create two capillaries with sharp tips (raw micropipettes).
Heat a raw pipette on the forge until the glass sphere melts, then insert the tip of the raw pipette inside the glass sphere.
Cool down the glass sphere and pull the raw pipette to break it from outside, leaving its tip inside the sphere.
Repeat heating, insertion, cooling, and breaking procedures until the desired tip orifice is obtained.
Cut a 40 mm x 22 mm x 0.2 mm coverslip into two 40 mm x 11 mm x 0.2 mm pieces (coverslip 1 and 2).
Glue coverslip 1 by grease to the top side of the chamber holder, bridging the two metal squares.
Glue coverslip 2 to the bottom side of the chamber holder, forming a parallel-coverslip cell chamber.
Inject 200 µl of experimental buffer between the two coverslips.
Ensure the buffer attaches to both coverslips.
Gently rotate and shake the chamber to ensure the buffer touches both ends of the chamber.
Carefully inject mineral oil into both sides of the chamber flanking the experimental buffer zone, sealing the buffer from open air.
Inject suspensions of probe beads in the upper region of the buffer zone.
Inject RBCs in the middle region of the buffer zone.
Inject targets (for example, T-cells) in the lower region of the buffer zone.
Turn on the microscope and light source.
Place the chamber onto the main microscope stage.
Install all three micropipettes for BFP (probe, target, helper).
Use a micro-injector to backfill a micropipette with experimental buffer.
Take off the pipette holder and hold it at a lower place to allow water dripping from the tip.
Insert the micropipette into the holder tip without introducing air bubbles.
Tighten the holder screw.
Mount each pipette holder onto its corresponding micro-manipulator.
Push the micropipette towards the chamber so that their tips enter the chamber buffer area.
Adjust the position of the micropipette and find them under the microscope field of view.
Move around the chamber holder stage to find the colonies of three elements (the RBCs, the targets, and the probe beads) one-by-one.
Adjust the position of the corresponding micropipette by turning the knobs of the manipulators to let the tip of the micropipette approach one cell/bead.
Aspirate the cell/bead by adjusting the pressure inside the corresponding micropipette.
Move around the chamber holder stage to find an open space away from the colonies of the injected elements where the experiment will be performed.
Switch the microscope visual mode to visualize the image on the computer program on the computer screen.
Move all three elements on pipette tips into the program’s vision field.
Align the probe bead and RBC, and carefully maneuver the probe bead to the apex of the RBC.
Briefly impinge the bead onto the RBC and gently retract.
Adjust the pressure of the helper micropipette to gently blow the bead away so that it will be left glued onto the RBC apex.
Move away the helper micropipette and align the target and probe bead.
Measure the radii of the probe micropipette using the tools in the program.
Measure the radius of the RBC using the tools in the program.
Measure the circular contact area between the RBC and probe bead using the tools in the program.
Estimate the spring constant of the RBC using the measured parameters.
Enter the desired RBC spring constant into the program.
Adjust the water tank height to reach the required aspiration pressure.
Draw a horizontal line across the RBC apex.
Drag the threshold line to around half the depth of the curve.
Turn on the excitation light source.
Turn on the fluorescence camera.
Select parameters for fluorescence imaging, including gain, exposure, and excitation channels (340 nm and 380 nm).
Align the probe with the target.
Section the area within which the cell will stay during the recording period.
Click on “Record” to alternate between 340 nm and 380 nm light excitations.
Begin the BFP experiment by clicking on “Start.”
Monitor intracellular calcium signaling through fluorescence imaging.
Sequentially inspect each cycle’s “force vs. time” signal.
Record which cycles contain an adhesion event and which do not.
Summarize to yield an average adhesion frequency.
Collect the rupture force of each adhesion event, which is the peak value of the linearly ramped force before bond rupture.
Derive the rupture force distribution at each ramp rate after collecting a sufficient amount of rupture forces in a range of ramp rates.
Use dynamic force spectroscopy analysis to derive the force-dependent off-rate of receptor-ligand dissociation from the rupture force distribution.
Inspect the clamping phase signal of each cycle sequentially.
Use the clamping phase thermal fluctuation level to distinguish bond association and dissociation events.
Designate the interval from bond dissociation to the next bond formation as waiting time.
Designate the duration of a bond from its association to dissociation as bond lifetime.
Calculate the average waiting time, reflecting the reciprocal of on-rate under zero-force.
Calculate the average bond lifetime, reflecting the reciprocal of off-rate under zero-force.
Record parameters of all lifetime events including the average force and bond lifetime with sequence number and timing details.
Draw a cumulative lifetime curve using recorded data.
Collect sufficient lifetime events under a range of forces.
Group collected events into different force bins to produce an average lifetime in each bin.
Yield an “average lifetime vs. force” curve from grouped data.
Adjust the intensity threshold until the fluorescence images show a clear cell contour in both 340 nm and 380 nm channels without background noise.
Review the intracellular Ca2+ signal frame by frame with a pseudo-color indicating the intensity level, which is derived from the intensity ratio of 340 nm/380 nm.
Generate the “normalized Ca2+ intensity vs. time” curve based on the reviewed frames.
Produce a movie displaying the fluorescence level second by second using the pseudo-color fluorescence images.
